questions.q: What should one consider first before taking a step against another group, according to the editorial?
options: The result it is likely to produce
Yes. If the result cannot be achieved, patience and adjustment are the course.
Whether one is in the right
Not quite. The article says: The result it is likely to produce.
What others will say
Not quite. The article says: The result it is likely to produce.
How many supporters one has
Not quite. The article says: The result it is likely to produce.
questions.rationale: “First of all, one should think about the result that this action would yield… if one is not in a position to attain the required result, then one must remain patient.”

questions.q: The Prophet said: “Evil is lying asleep. The curse of God is on one who awakens it.” How does the editorial apply this?
options: One should sleep rather than argue
Not quite. The article says: Do not let differences grow into confrontation, for the one who begins it bears the blame for what follows.
Evil people should be left unpunished
Not quite. The article says: Do not let differences grow into confrontation, for the one who begins it bears the blame for what follows.
Do not let differences grow into confrontation, for the one who begins it bears the blame for what follows
Right. Confrontation “does not know the language of justice.”
Evil does not exist until it is named
Not quite. The article says: Do not let differences grow into confrontation, for the one who begins it bears the blame for what follows.
questions.rationale: “If we want to save ourselves from the ill effects of evil, then we must try our utmost to avoid awakening it. The beginner is the one who is responsible for the aftermath.”

questions.q: The article compares adjustment to keeping to one’s side of the road. What is the point?
options: Adjustment is practical wisdom that keeps one’s own journey going; it is not submission
Yes. “When you are not in the position to change others, change yourself.”
The slower driver must always give way
Not quite. The article says: Adjustment is practical wisdom that keeps one’s own journey going; it is not submission.
Everyone should travel the same way
Not quite. The article says: Adjustment is practical wisdom that keeps one’s own journey going; it is not submission.
Rules exist to be obeyed without thought
Not quite. The article says: Adjustment is practical wisdom that keeps one’s own journey going; it is not submission.
questions.rationale: “Adjustment is not a submissive attitude; rather it is an attitude of wisdom… Adjustment gives you a chance to continue your journey.”

questions.q: “Men and nations do the sensible thing only after they have exhausted all other options.” What does the article say about accepting truth only when forced?
options: Such acceptance has no value – and on the Day of Reckoning it will come too late
Exactly. Worth lies in choosing rightly while free.
It is the only way people ever learn
Not quite. The article says: Such acceptance has no value – and on the Day of Reckoning it will come too late.
It is as good as accepting it freely
Not quite. The article says: Such acceptance has no value – and on the Day of Reckoning it will come too late.
It shows strength of character
Not quite. The article says: Such acceptance has no value – and on the Day of Reckoning it will come too late.
questions.rationale: “If one accepts the truth because one is forced to, one’s acceptance has no value.”

questions.q: Aisha related that the first verses revealed were about God and the Hereafter, and commands came later. What method does the article draw from this?
options: Laws must be enforced before beliefs are taught
Not quite. The article says: Reform begins with minds and hearts; rules follow once people are ready.
Reform begins with minds and hearts; rules follow once people are ready
Well reasoned. Otherwise people would have refused outright.
Belief makes laws unnecessary
Not quite. The article says: Reform begins with minds and hearts; rules follow once people are ready.
Commands should be revealed all at once
Not quite. The article says: Reform begins with minds and hearts; rules follow once people are ready.
questions.rationale: “The enforcement of Shariah law begins in any society with intellectual purification of individuals, rather than with the practical enforcement of law.”

questions.q: What change does the article describe in a person who begins to live for God?
options: He withdraws from family and work
Not quite. The article says: He prefers silence to talk, forgiveness to grudges, and has no wish for a privileged place.
He prefers silence to talk, forgiveness to grudges, and has no wish for a privileged place
Yes. He becomes unassuming.
He seeks to lead others
Not quite. The article says: He prefers silence to talk, forgiveness to grudges, and has no wish for a privileged place.
He grows stern towards those who differ
Not quite. The article says: He prefers silence to talk, forgiveness to grudges, and has no wish for a privileged place.
questions.rationale: “He finds silence more gratifying than speech. He is happier to obey than to rebel, to forgive than to hold grudges… He is unassuming and self-effacing.”

questions.q: The article calls the Prophet’s migration to Madinah “changing the place of activity.” What principle does it take from it?
options: One should never leave one’s homeland
Not quite. The article says: When work is blocked in one place, look for a more favourable setting; do not fight on to destruction.
Opposition must be met where it arises
Not quite. The article says: When work is blocked in one place, look for a more favourable setting; do not fight on to destruction.
When work is blocked in one place, look for a more favourable setting; do not fight on to destruction
Right. The move brought expansion, not escape.
A mission should be paused in hard times
Not quite. The article says: When work is blocked in one place, look for a more favourable setting; do not fight on to destruction.
questions.rationale: “The desired course of action is not to remain at the same place, while pursuing an escalating and disastrous conflict… the desire should be to search out an alternative and conducive atmosphere.”

questions.q: What does the article mean by “changing the field of activity,” seen in the Treaty of Hudaibiya?
options: Moving the contest from the battlefield to the peaceful exchange of ideas
Yes. Many then came to the Prophet’s message.
Turning from trade to farming
Not quite. The article says: Moving the contest from the battlefield to the peaceful exchange of ideas.
Moving the capital to another city
Not quite. The article says: Moving the contest from the battlefield to the peaceful exchange of ideas.
Replacing old leaders with new ones
Not quite. The article says: Moving the contest from the battlefield to the peaceful exchange of ideas.
questions.rationale: “After this peace treaty, the field of confrontation between the two sides was replaced by the ideological field.”

questions.q: Why does the article say failure can be “greater than success”?
options: Failure costs less effort
Not quite. The article says: Success breeds contentment, while failure stirs a drive that brings out hidden abilities.
Success is always a matter of luck
Not quite. The article says: Success breeds contentment, while failure stirs a drive that brings out hidden abilities.
Success breeds contentment, while failure stirs a drive that brings out hidden abilities
Well read. Khorana, B. C. Roy and Bill Gates are the examples.
Failure wins the sympathy of others
Not quite. The article says: Success breeds contentment, while failure stirs a drive that brings out hidden abilities.
questions.rationale: “If you gain success, you become content. However, if you experience failure, then it generates great motivation in you.”

questions.article: All Credit Goes to God Almighty
questions.q: When success comes, to whom should the credit be given, and why does it matter?
options: To God, who gave the person and every means he used; each success is a test of this recognition
Correct. To credit anyone else is to fail the test.
To oneself, for the effort made
Not quite. The article says: To God, who gave the person and every means he used; each success is a test of this recognition.
To good fortune
Not quite. The article says: To God, who gave the person and every means he used; each success is a test of this recognition.
To one’s rivals, out of courtesy
Not quite. The article says: To God, who gave the person and every means he used; each success is a test of this recognition.
questions.rationale: “It is God Almighty who has created the successful person… If a person gives the credit to the Creator, then he passes his test.”
